 Motley Fool: Sweet dividends with Mondelez
 Sun., Oct. 25, 2026 
 Mondelez International is the company behind several household names, including Toblerone. (Stephen Kelly/Bloomerg)
 Add Spokesman-Review on Google
 Andrews McMeel Syndication
 Mondelez International (Nasdaq: MDLZ) is a leading multinational confectionery and snacking company with a recent market valuation of $80 billion. Its portfolio includes cookies, crackers, protein bars, chocolates, chewing gum and candies, generating substantial revenue across multiple geographic markets worldwide. Mondelez’s brands include Cadbury, Clif Bar, Oreo, Ritz, Tate’s Bake Shop, Toblerone and Triscuit.
 The company’s competitive positioning is reinforced by its diversified product portfolio, established brand recognition and extensive distribution network spanning six continents. With 91,000 employees and a recent net profit margin of 8.9%, Mondelez demonstrates operational efficiency and consistent profitability.
 Its stock has a forward-looking price-to-earnings ratio of under 19, slightly below its five-year average of 20. And the stock’s recent dividend yield is appealing at 3.4%. That dividend has also been growing, with a 4% hike announced in July.
 Mondelez International isn’t likely to soar, but it is likely to keep growing, while rewarding shareholders over time. In its second quarter, revenue was up 4.1% year over year. A drop in cocoa prices could also provide a tailwind.
 Long-term investors might want to take a closer look at Mondelez.
 Ask the fool
 Q. What’s a derivative? – F.B., Chugiak, Alaska 
 A. It’s a financial contract between you and another party with a value tied to that of one or more underlying assets or benchmarks; these might be stocks, bonds, interest rates, market indexes, mortgages or currencies. There are many kinds of derivatives of varying complexity, including options, futures and forwards, swaps and collateralized debt obligations . Derivatives can lock in prices and may help you hedge against possible losses, but they can also be hard to value and quite risky. Warren Buffett once called them “financial weapons of mass destruction.”
 Q. What are Roth IRAs? – D.M., Naperville, Illinois 
 A. Individual retirement arrangements come in two main varieties: traditional and Roth. Contributions to a traditional IRA can reduce your taxable income for the year, shrinking your tax bill. So if you earn $77,500 and contribute $7,500, your taxable income drops to $70,000. When you withdraw the money in retirement, it will be taxed as ordinary income.
 With contributions to a Roth Fool’s IRA, there’s no up-front tax break, but if you follow the rules, your eventual withdrawls can be can be completely tax free. If you contribute a lot to your account over many years, investing that money effectively, you might end up with hundreds of thousands of dollars in your account – all available tax-free in retirement.
 For 2026, contribution limits for traditional and Roth IRAs are $7,500 per person, plus an additional $1,100 for those 50 and older. Note that the contribution deadline for IRAs each year is not Dec. 31, but the tax filing deadline for the year. So contributions for 2026 can be made until mid-April of 2027. Learn more in our “Retirement” nook at Fool.com.
 My dumbest investment
 My most regrettable investment was undoubtedly Global Crossing. That sucker ate my lunch, dinner and breakfast the next day! – P., online
 The Fool responds: Ouch. When Global Crossing filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 2002, it was one of the biggest companies ever to do so. Founded in 1997, it built a fiber-optic cable network around the world, connecting over 200 major cities in 27 countries, in part via undersea cables. But it took on a lot of debt to do so, and demand was not as high as expected. Meanwhile, the internet bubble burst, creating an unhelpful business climate. Global Crossing was also embroiled in multiple lawsuits and government investigations alleging improper accounting. The company eventually emerged from bankruptcy and was later acquired by Level 3 Communications – but as you know, its prebankruptcy shareholders and thousands of employees ended up with little to nothing.
 While many companies emerge from bankruptcy and go on to great success, their prebankruptcy shareholders typically suffer significant or total losses. If you’re invested in a struggling company, especially one in legal trouble, dig into its chances of survival and consider selling. You may be able to get out while its shares still have some value.
 (Do you have a smart or regrettable investment move to share with us? Email it to TMFShare@fool.com.)
